title: Psychology mini-dissertation 2026/27
text:
Project keywords

statistical learning
transitional probabilities
neurodiversity
autism
behavioural experiment



Project background
Humans are very good at learning sequences: for example, the sequences of notes that combine to make songs, or the sequences of syllables that combine to make words. The key cognitive process that helps humans learn sequences is called “statistical learning” (it has nothing to do with learning how to do stats!). As you experience a sequence of syllables, for example, you’ll gradually develop a sense that, if you hear a certain syllable, you can make a reasonable guess about what syllable will come next. That sense means that you’re learning the distributional statistics of the sequence. In other words, it means you’re doing statistical learning (see, e.g., Saffran et al., 1996; Isbilen & Christiansen, 2022).
A more concrete example: think about the English sequence “pretty baby”, which sound something like “prih-tee bay-bee”. After you’ve heard “prih”, there aren’t many syllables that can come next and make a good English word. “Mih”, maybe, for “primitive”, or “tee” for “pretty” (maybe you can think of other ones!). We say that the syllable sequence “prih-tee” has a high transitional probability. This is because the probability that “tee” comes after “prih” is relatively high (or: once you’ve heard “prih”, you can predict fairly confidently what syllable will come next).
In contrast, after you’ve heard “tee”, you’re at the end of the word, and there are a lot of English syllables that can come next. “Good”, “cat”, “bay” … we say that the syllable sequence “tee-bay” has a low transitional probability, because the probability that “bay” comes after “tee” is relatively low (or: once you’ve heard “tee”, you can’t really predict very confidently what will come next).
Now let’s bring in the autism angle. Autistic cognition is characterised by locally-oriented sensory processing (reflecting what’s commonly called “attention to detail”) and a preference for predictable input (see, e.g., Mottron et al., 2006; Van de Cruys et al., 2014). In light of this, we want to know: how does autistic cognition impact statistical learning?
Importantly, throughout this project, we will consider autism as a difference in cognition that results from natural variation, rather than a deficit, in line with neurodiversity-positive approaches (see, e.g., Manalili et al., 2023; Walker & Raymaker, 2021).
We know that autistic people are just as good at statistical learning as allistic (non-autistic) people (see, e.g., Obeid et al., 2016; Haebig et al., 2017). But we want to dig in deeper. Based on previous research, we expect that people will be better at recognising syllable sequences that have higher transitional probabilities, compared to sequences with lower transitional probabilities (see, e.g., Pankratz et al., 2024). But for the syllable sequences with low transitional probabilities:

do autistic people learn them better than allistic people, because of autistic people’s superior processing of local dependencies?
Or do autistic people learn them worse than allistic people, because autistic people are more disrupted by the unpredictable input?

More broadly, the research question that will guide our project is:

Are people less accurate at recognising lower-probability syllable sequences compared to higher-probability ones, and is this difference affected by people’s level of autistic traits?

To answer this question, we will run a behavioural statistical learning experiment using Testable, ask participants to fill in the AQ10 questionnaire (Allison et al., 2012), and analyse the results using a logistic mixed-effects regression model (you’ll learn about mixed-effects models with me in DAPR3).

title: Project FAQs
text:
Lit review

What’s the point of a lit review?

To give your readers the necessary context for your research.
To motivate why your research question is interesting.
To explain why you make the predictions that you make.



How do we know what’s important to say about a given paper?

Try the following three-step process (hat tip to Dr. Joléne van der Mescht):

What did the authors do? (their question and methods)
What did they find? (their results, prioritising what’s relevant for your RQ)
Your critical comment / evaluation / “so what?”, for example:

What implications do their findings have?
How do their findings relate to other papers’ findings?
What predictions would you make for your RQ, based on their results?





How do we know what order to put ideas in?

A good general strategy:

Identify the key message(s) of each paper you want to mention.
Write down all the pieces of information that are needed for understanding the key messages (all keywords, main topics, etc.)
Group together the pieces of information that show up repeatedly in different papers.
Think: Which of those pieces of information are needed for understanding other pieces of information? Which pieces of information can stand alone?
Try to put all the pieces of information in an order that builds the reader’s understanding. Use each piece of information as a stepping stone toward the next piece of information.

If the research question combines a couple different ideas (let’s call the ideas A and B), then a good three-part structure is often:

What do we know about A? (Prioritise the detail that’s relevant for the RQ)

e.g., statistical learning in general
relevant detail: transitional probabilities (TPs) can be different

What do we know about B? (Prioritise the detail that’s relevant for the RQ)

e.g., autism in general
relevant detail: local processing has priority over global processing

What do we know, and what do we wonder, about how A and B come together? Based on the information from Sections 1 and 2, what predictions can we make?

e.g., that autistic people might use distributional cues like TPs differently than allistic people do, because autistic people prioritise lower-level local information





How many papers do we need to cite?

There’s no set number that means you’ve cited enough papers.
The more papers you read and interact with, the stronger and more well-founded your argument will be.



How much literature is enough? How do we know when to stop reading?

Double-check that you’ve covered all the widely-cited key papers (e.g., by searching keywords on Google Scholar and looking for papers cited >100 or especially >1000 times).
After that: you’ve probably read enough when all the claims that you want to make are justified/supported by the literature.

title: Project FAQs
text:
Research report

How many words should the introduction / methods / results / discussion / conclusion section have?

There’s no set number of words for each section.
Focus more on saying everything that you want to say, rather than the specific length of each section.
If in doubt, I recommend that you start by writing too much, and then you can trim it down later.



Do we need to submit analysis code?

Nope!
You just need to report/explain your analysis clearly enough that someone else could replicate it fully without seeing your code (like in the DAPR reports).



Can we include figures/plots in the Discussion section?

Depends on the goal of the figure/plot!
The Discussion section is for interpreting results, not introducing new results.
So if your figure is meant to help the reader interpret your findings, then yes absolutely.



Can the minidiss have a different title than the lit review / poster?

Yes, please!
Customise your title to the research story you’re trying to tell.
I like titles that are a full (but short) sentence that declare the research finding, e.g., “Autistic traits are associated with [X]”.



Do words in figures, tables, and their captions count toward the word count total?

Nope. You can include as many words there as you like.



Do words in the abstract count toward the word count total?

Nope. The abstract should be max 150 words, and the report should be max 2000 words, so between the two, you have max 2150 words.
